lessons.title: Build a profile from components
lessons.summary: Compose a profile from a component, pass details as props, and update a local counter.
explanation:
React builds interfaces from components. A component is a function that returns a description of what should appear. JSX is the HTML-like notation inside JavaScript, such as

Hello

. A JSX-aware runner translates it before execution. These examples use the lesson's available React object; they need React and JSX support, so they cannot be pasted unchanged into a plain JavaScript console.

Capitalized <Profile ... /> asks React to use your component; lowercase <section> describes a built-in HTML element. name="Tara" passes text. Curly braces inside JSX evaluate JavaScript: {props.name} inserts the actual name. Text outside braces, such as Learning, appears literally. The closing /> means this component call has no enclosed children. A returned tree needs one surrounding element, here main.

State is data React remembers between renders. A render is React calling components to work out the current interface. setTaps asks React to render with the updated state; it does not directly rewrite the button's HTML. The arrow () => ... creates a function for a future click. Passing that function matters: calling setTaps while building the screen would update during rendering instead of waiting for the user.

current => current + 1 is a functional update: React supplies the latest queued count. Calling setCount(count + 1) also works for the exercise's separate clicks, but functional updates help when several increments are queued together. An ordinary local let variable would reset when the function runs again and would not itself tell React to render. Call hooks such as useState at the top level of the component, not inside a condition.

For the exercise, preserve Mina's Swift profile and the Practice button's label. Each click increments only count. Starting from 0, three taps follow 0 → 1 → 2 → 3; adding one each time is counting, not multiplication. A changing counter should not change read-only profile props. In larger apps, define child components outside their parent to preserve stable component identity; the starter's nested Profile is adequate for this simple stateless example.

analogy.connection: Props are like the name printed on a badge; state is like a tally you can change while using the page.
analogy.limit: A component should not change its incoming props, just as a guest should not rewrite a printed badge.

steps: Create Profile with name "Mina" and subject "Swift". Show Mina in an h2 heading and "Learning Swift" in a paragraph.
Start count at 0 and display "Practice taps: 0". Label the counter button "Practice".
Increase count once per click. Two clicks should show "Practice taps: 2" while the profile text stays the same.

choices: The profile shows Learning Drawing; the counter keeps its value

lessons.title: Build an activity board
lessons.summary: Handle a labeled form, reject empty submissions, and show each valid entry once.
explanation: React handles actions through event-handler functions. A controlled input takes its displayed value from state and updates that state when someone types. value sets the displayed text; onChange tells React how to respond to edits. You need both. A visible label tells people what the field is for, including people using assistive technology. This isolated preview does not enable native form submission. Use Run checks to exercise the handler here; test submit-button and Enter-key behavior in a normal browser setup.

Forms normally submit by navigating or reloading the page. event.preventDefault() prevents that default action so your React code can handle submission. It does not stop typing. trim() removes whitespace from both ends of a string. Three spaces become empty text, whose length is 0. A valid submission here needs trimmed length greater than 0, so a blank draft must be rejected before anything is added.

The early return stops the invalid path. [...current, cleaned] creates a new array by spreading the existing items, then appending the cleaned text. It preserves earlier notes and gives React a new value to render. map visits each note and returns one li element. key helps React track list children; an index key is acceptable for this simple append-only list, but stable unique ids are better for lists that reorder or remove items.

role="status" exposes the message as status feedback for assistive technology. type="submit" connects the button to the form's submit action, so pressing Enter in the field can also submit. Attach addition to the form handler once; adding in both an onClick and onSubmit can duplicate items. The handler receives a function reference submit, rather than submit(), which would run immediately.

For the exercise, the field label is Activity, the button is Add activity, and the required messages are Enter an activity first. and Activity added. Keep those words because the checks inspect visible behavior. Reject a blank or whitespace-only draft, add a valid trimmed item exactly once, then clear draft. Clearing a message alone does not clear the input: the controlled field follows its own state.

analogy.connection: A controlled field is like a clipboard where the displayed text follows the current form value.
analogy.limit: A form should keep its label visible so people know what belongs in the field.

Add a labeled input. Make the form run a submit function when the user submits it.
Submit an empty field. Add no list item and show "Enter an activity first."
Enter "  Read  " with spaces at the edges, then submit once.
Check that the list has one item, "Read", with the outside spaces removed.
Clear the input and show "Activity added." after adding the item.

choices: Yes, because the original length is 3

lessons.title: Build an accessible disclosure
lessons.summary: Build a menu with clear labels, keyboard actions, and predictable focus return.
explanation: Keyboard access means someone can use a feature without a mouse. Native buttons can receive focus with Tab and activate with Enter or Space. Focus is the control that currently receives keyboard input. Give buttons a visible name describing their action and keep focus visible. A clickable div would need extra keyboard behavior that a button already provides.

In JSX, {open && ...} renders the element when open is true. !value flips a boolean: false becomes true. We also need a deliberate focus plan. Opening should focus the first action after it exists; Escape should close and return focus to the trigger. A ref stores a reference to an actual DOM element without needing a render every time it changes.

useRef(null) starts without an element; React fills .current when the ref's button is mounted. ?. means only call focus when the current value exists. useEffect runs its work after React has committed the screen update, so the first button is available. [open] is the dependency array: run this effect when open changes. Setting a ref does not itself update the visible screen.

Key events bubble from a focused child to its ancestor, allowing nav's handler to see Escape from a list button. The close function hides the list and restores the trigger as the keyboard position. Tab is still ordinary focus navigation. This is a simple disclosure containing native buttons, not a full ARIA menu widget; adding role="menu" would require additional expected keyboard behavior such as arrow-key navigation.

For the exercise, the trigger's visible name must be Activities, aria-controls must point to activity-menu, and opening must focus Start practice. Escape closes and returns focus to Activities. Test it with Tab, Enter or Space, then Escape. Confirm the expanded attribute changes with state and focus really moves. This unit has no math question; the learning task is the interaction itself.

analogy.connection: A menu button is like a clearly labeled remote button that opens a small list of choices.
analogy.limit: A visible menu is not enough; keyboard users also need a clear path into and back out of it.

Start aria-expanded at false and set aria-controls to "activity-menu".
Show the choices only when the menu is open. After opening it, move keyboard focus to the first choice.
When Escape is pressed, close the menu and move keyboard focus back to the Activities button.

lessons.title: Build a reading dashboard
lessons.summary: Use shared state and explicit loading, empty, error, and success views across dashboard screens.
explanation: A dashboard can show different views of one shared dataset. Store the selected view and loaded records in the common parent component so switching views preserves them. Home and Saved here are local screen choices; they do not change the browser URL or maintain separate saved records. The loader is a simulation, so no server or secret is needed.

Loading means waiting for a result. Empty means a successful result with no records. Error means the attempt failed. Success with records means the list is ready. Idle means no attempt yet. Treating all these cases as one blank list hides useful information. A role="alert" message can announce an error; a list of real results should appear only in the successful state.

++latest.current adds one and supplies that new number as this attempt's id. A ref retains this counter across renders without causing an extra render. setTimeout schedules the callback after a delay in milliseconds; 1,000 milliseconds is one second. Each callback keeps the id and mode from its own call. Before changing either results or errors, compare that id with the newest one.

Click Slow sample and then Error sample before the slow result arrives. The later error owns the current id, so its message remains; the old success is ignored. Reverse the kinds of outcomes and the same rule should protect a later success from an old error. For example, request 2 succeeds and request 1 later fails: keep request 2's success. Checking only successful responses would still let stale errors break the screen.

For your exercise, combine shared navigation with the loader and preserve the supplied labels and messages. Include Load sample, Load empty, Load error, and Load older slow result. Sample success shows A Field Guide; empty success says No books yet.; error says Books could not be loaded. Show Loading books… while waiting. Keep view independent of load state so Home/Saved preserves the current dataset. A real fetch loader must also check response status and guard both success and failure against stale ids.

analogy.connection: The dashboard is like a library desk that can show a shelf, a loading note, an empty shelf, or an explanation when the catalog is unavailable.
analogy.limit: Changing screens does not cancel a real request by itself; code must handle stale responses.

Make Saved change the heading to "Saved books". Make Home change it back to "Reading".
Use the same books list in both views.
Add four buttons: Load sample, Load empty, Load error, and Load older slow result.
Show the loading message before each result.
For a successful sample load, show "A Field Guide". For an empty result, show "No books yet."
For a failed load, show "Books could not be loaded."
Wait 100 ms for the slow response and 15 ms for normal responses.
Give each request an ID. Ignore a result if a newer request has started.
Click Load older slow result, then immediately click Load error. The later error must stay visible.

lessons.title: Explore a large list efficiently
lessons.summary: Filter a large fixed list, count examined rows, and preserve the same results while reducing repeated work.
explanation: Filtering a list examines each item to decide whether it matches. If there are n items and you inspect each once, that is linear work, written O(n). The O notation describes how work grows, not an exact clock time. Growing a list from 1,000 to 8,000 items means roughly eight times as many comparisons for the same full scan.

React may render again for a state update that does not affect the query or list. useMemo remembers a calculated result while its dependency values remain the same. A dependency is an input that can change the answer. It does not make a new query constant-time; a changed query still needs a scan. React compares each dependency with its previous value, so keeping the array itself stable matters too.

To compare work across renders, the exercise records each newly committed calculation result. A ref stores previous baseline and memoized object references and running counts. Its effect depends on the two result objects. If a result reference changed, add that result's examined count; then store the new references and put totals into state. The totals render does not change items, query, or repeat, so it does not create a measuring loop.

Exclude repeat from the memoized dependencies but retain items and query. Initially each calculation represents 1,000 comparisons. After repeating unchanged inputs once, the baseline total becomes 2,000 while the memoized total stays 1,000, with identical match arrays. The check's totals assume this supplied run without development StrictMode. Extra development or discarded renders can make raw execution counts different. useMemo is a performance aid whose cache React may discard; correct results must not depend on retaining it.

analogy.connection: A list filter is like checking each card for a matching word; skipping a repeated check can save effort when the cards did not change.
analogy.limit: Memoization uses memory and only helps when the inputs repeat; it is not automatically faster for every small list.

Use the effect to add up the actual comparisons after each new calculation.
After one repeat, expect a baseline total of 2,000 and a memoized total of 1,000.
Check that both filters still return the same matches.

lessons.title: Test search races and failures
lessons.summary: Build a search view that ignores stale responses and keeps loading and error states understandable.
explanation: Asynchronous search can finish in a different order from when searches started. If A starts first but B finishes first, B may be the result the person now wants. A late success or failure from A must not replace it. Give each search a new id, store the latest id in a ref, and compare ids before applying either outcome.

In React, a controlled input keeps query in state. Each search handler uses the query from the render that supplied that handler. A callback created inside the handler keeps that snapshot, even if the person types a different query later. A request id decides whether the snapshot is still current. Typing alone need not start a request; pressing Search does in this exercise.

Check both race orders. Start a slow error, then a quick success: keep the success after the old error arrives. Start a slow success, then a quick error: keep the error and show no old list after the success arrives. Using the id check at the beginning of the callback protects both. Clearing error when a new search begins avoids displaying the old failure as though the new attempt already failed.

A useful interface test types into the actual input and activates the actual buttons, then waits long enough for the sample timers and inspects the visible outcome. It should cover loading, empty success, normal success, failure, and both stale-response orders. Testing only the existence of a search function or a particular variable name would miss a broken visible flow.

For the exercise, preserve Search books, Search, Fail search, Searching…, No results., and Search failed. Try again. Format successful rows as Result for followed by the captured query. A newer B success remains visible when older A fails; the math question is reasoning about event order, not calculating delay totals. The supplied timers simulate requests; replacing them with fetch requires the same current-id protection in both success and catch/error paths.

analogy.connection: A request ID is like an order number that prevents an old plate from replacing the newest order at the table.
analogy.limit: The ID prevents stale display updates; it does not stop the network request from using time or resources.

After failure, show "Search failed. Try again."
Try an empty successful search and a normal successful search.
Start a slow failing search, then a fast successful search. Keep the newer success.
Start a slow successful search, then a fast failing search. Keep the newer failure.
